ratings.killer: Incremental translation of existing evals; gap exists only due to resource prioritization, not fundamental scientific interest.
Tokenization and script-based evasion are well-documented in jailbreaking; applying it to scheming is a trivial extension.
Code-switching as an evasion tactic is already heavily studied in multilingual safety literature.
Ambitious but MechInterp across languages is notoriously confounded by tokenization; hard to isolate true semantic circuits.
Pure replication of Anthropic's work in new languages. Reviewers will immediately flag as lacking algorithmic novelty.
Extremely hard to operationalize cleanly; highly confounded by RLHF cultural bias and training data distributions.
Strong, testable hypothesis that English artifacts trigger eval-awareness. Could fundamentally improve how we measure scheming.
LLMs lack persistent internal state; entirely confounded by in-context token conditioning rather than actual cognitive dissonance.
Context-window dependence makes this indistinguishable from standard prompt-injection or multi-turn jailbreak dynamics.
Multi-agent persona framing and social simulacra are heavily saturated topics in recent NLP literature.
Standard psychology replication on LLMs. Reviewers are exhausted by 'LLMs exhibit human bias X' papers.
Prospect theory and loss aversion in LLMs have been done to death. Zero novelty.
LLM self-evaluation bias and failure to self-correct are already extensively documented in recent literature.
Another basic cognitive bias test. Lacks AI-safety relevance and mechanistic depth.
Shutdown resistance is relevant, but 'mortality salience' framing is heavily confounded by sci-fi tropes in pretraining.
Graduated compliance is already the core mechanism of multi-turn jailbreaks like Crescendo. Not novel.
Literally describes existing multi-turn jailbreak literature. The gap is entirely non-existent.

overall: Track A is far stronger. Track B is saturated with low-effort 'psychology of LLMs' papers. I7 offers a genuinely novel, testable mechanism for improving scheming evals by removing English-centric awareness cues.
